steps.en: What you see: A mobile echogenic mass on a leaflet moves independently from the valve with a shimmering chaotic motion. Abscess cavities hollow the aortic root in invasive disease. New regurgitation jets through perforated leaflets, and a prosthetic valve may rock with dehiscence. Transoesophageal imaging sees vegetations that the chest wall hides, so a negative transthoracic study never rules out disease when suspicion is high.

Normal values with units: Vegetation size. Small below 10 mm with no abscess. Moderate 10 to 15 mm. Severe above 15 mm with high embolic risk, or any abscess, severe regurgitation or heart failure.. Source: ASE and SCA 2013 transoesophageal examination guideline, section on endocarditis imaging

Timing of repeat imaging. Repeat in 7 to 10 days when clinical suspicion persists after a negative study.. Source: ASE and SCA 2013 transoesophageal examination guideline, section on endocarditis imaging

Prosthetic valve assessment. Any new paravalvular jet with rocking motion of the prosthesis marks dehiscence and needs surgical review.. Source: ASE 2017 valvular regurgitation guideline, section on paravalvular leaks

ECG and heart sound correlation ecg: New atrioventricular block warns of aortic root abscess invading the conduction tissue and is an emergency. Non specific ST changes can follow coronary embolism. Atrial fibrillation is uncommon and suggests another cause.

ECG and heart sound correlation sounds: A new regurgitant murmur that was absent before is the classic clue. The murmur changes as leaflet destruction progresses. A pericardial rub suggests spread to the sac.

What to report: Vegetation position, size in two planes, mobility and attachment site
Abscess, perforation, fistula or prosthetic dehiscence with measurements
Regurgitation grade with chamber sizes and pulmonary pressure
Comparison with the last study: growth, shrinkage or new destruction
Red flags needing urgent referral: New heart block with aortic root thickening, needs emergency surgical review for abscess
Severe regurgitation with heart failure or shock, needs emergency surgical review
Recurrent emboli or a highly mobile vegetation above 15 mm, needs urgent surgical review
Pitfalls: Rheumatic scarred valves in Indian patients seed easily, so suspect endocarditis early in any febrile valve patient.
Fungal and culture negative disease follows prior antibiotics, so record every dose before cultures.
Brain, splenic and renal emboli hide outside the heart, so examine beyond the chest in every case.

todo.en: How to get it on the probe, step by step: Start transthoracic in long axis and short axis with a high frequency probe and low gain.
Zoom each valve and watch for masses with motion independent from the leaflet.
Measure the vegetation at its largest in two planes and note mobility and stalk.
Look for abscess cavities at the aortic root, new regurgitation and prosthetic rocking.
Proceed to transoesophageal imaging when suspicion stays high despite a negative surface study.

Common mistakes and how to correct them: Calling Lambl excrescences or strands vegetations. Fix: Vegetations attach on the low pressure side and move chaotically, while strands move with the leaflet. Watch two cycles zoomed.
Starting antibiotics before cultures in a stable patient. Fix: Take blood cultures before antibiotics whenever the patient is stable enough, since sterile cultures blind therapy.
Ruling out disease on one early negative study. Fix: Repeat imaging in 7 to 10 days when suspicion persists, since early vegetations are below resolution.

remember.en: Act on heart block, heart failure and emboli as surgical emergencies.

why.en: Independent chaotic shimmer separates vegetations from strands that ride with the leaflet.

q.en: Which finding pushes toward urgent surgical review?

o.en: Above 15 mm or any abscess with heart failure

why.en: Large highly mobile vegetations above 15 mm, abscess, severe regurgitation and heart failure are surgical triggers.

q.en: New complete heart block appears with aortic root thickening. What next?

why.en: Block marks abscess invasion of conduction tissue and needs emergency surgical review.

q.en: A stable febrile patient shows a new mobile mass. What is the order?

o.en: Take blood cultures first when stable, then start therapy fast
Wait for the vegetation to shrink alone

why.en: Cultures before antibiotics preserve the microbiological diagnosis whenever stability allows.

q.en: The first transthoracic study is negative but suspicion stays high. What next?

o.en: Repeat in 7 to 10 days if suspicion persists
It proves a non cardiac fever

why.en: Early vegetations sit below resolution, so repeat imaging and transoesophageal study follow persistent suspicion.
